claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure containing fcc and hexagonal C14 Laves phases.
The alloy has ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Coexistence of the C14 phase enhances coercivity to approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
Strong antiferromagnetic coupling occurs between a Ti-rich C14 sublattice and Fe/Co/Ni sublattices in the fcc matrix.
The proposed interphase antiferromagnetic coupling suppresses the net magnetic moment and saturation magnetization of the fcc phase.
The fcc/C14 interfaces provide a high density of magnetic domain-wall pinning sites.
The fcc phase remains ferromagnetically ordered at 400 K.
At 400 K, the C14 phase may be antiferromagnetic or weakly ferromagnetic and capable of coupling to the fcc phase.
The C14 lattice in this alloy is Ti-rich.
Antiferromagnetic exchange specifically involves Ti 3d states in C14 and Fe/Co/Ni 3d states in fcc.
The C14 phase is sufficiently rigid to contribute to interfacial barriers.
Local magnetic anisotropy develops at fcc/C14 interfaces.
Interfacial anisotropy and C14-related barriers impede domain-wall motion and thereby increase coercivity.
Single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi or Fe-Co-Ni has coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and weak pinning.
The dual-phase alloy will have lower saturation magnetization than a single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi comparator.
Interfacial coupling will shift the magnetic transition temperatures.
The mechanism requires the C14 phase to retain a magnetic moment capable of coupling to the fcc phase at 400 K.
The magnetic ordering of C14 FeCoNiTi at 400 K and the magnitude of its interfacial exchange constant are unknown.
Element-specific XMCD at Ti and Fe/Co/Ni L-edges can test whether Ti moments align antiparallel to the transition-metal moments.
Comparison of dual-phase and C14-suppressed single-fcc samples can test whether C14 correlates with enhanced coercivity and reduced saturation magnetization.
